summary: A guide to using Telnet to reach UCSB's Online System. It explains why and how the system was connected, its limitations, the virtual keyboard, and local commands such as help, prefix, shift, duplex mode and logout. It includes examples of logging on and instructing the user Telnet program.

plainLanguage.summary: An instruction sheet for visiting a special computer at the university from far away by typing over the network. It lists the keys and commands you can use and shows sample sessions.

subtitle: Guide to accessing UCSB's mathematical computing system through Telnet

tldr.problem: UCSB's powerful Online System (OLS) was designed for interactive terminals with special keyboards and graphical display capabilities. Telnet users had only plain text, so a mapping system was needed.
tldr.mechanism: NETOLS, a network front-end to OLS, maps Telnet characters to OLS keyboard keys and handles special commands. Standard keys map one-to-one, while non-standard keys are entered via a prefix character followed by a key name and space. Graphical and special character display are suppressed for text-only compatibility.
tldr.outcome: Network users can access UCSB's OLS for mathematical computing, though with limitations. Curvilinear and graphical features are disabled, and operations assuming a fixed-screen display work differently.

today: This implementation pioneered network access to sophisticated computational systems, demonstrating how Telnet could bridge text-based remote terminals to graphical systems, a pattern that influenced remote computing for decades.

sections.title: Network Access to OLS
sections.content:
UCSB's Online System (OLS) is a mathematical computing tool with powerful graphical display capabilities, designed to be used with a specialized double keyboard. NETOLS provides network access via Telnet, allowing remote users to access OLS though some features are unavailable in text-only mode.

NETOLS listens on socket 1 at UCSB (host address 3). When a network user connects, NETOLS establishes a duplex Telnet connection and acquires a port on OLS. It then initiates a login sequence by simulating pressing the SYST key, and stays active for the duration of the connection as an interpreter between Telnet input and OLS.
sections.plainLanguage: A gateway program lets remote terminals use a big mathematics computer, converting typed commands into the special keyboard the computer expects.

sections.title: The Virtual Keyboard
sections.content:
NETOLS maps Telnet characters to OLS keyboard keys. The lower keyboard maps mostly one-to-one: uppercase letters become lowercase, and standard punctuation maps to itself. The upper keyboard keys and non-standard keys are accessed via a prefix character (default is semicolon) followed by the key name and space.

For example, with the default prefix, the SIN (sine) key is entered as ;SIN , which can be abbreviated as ;SI if unambiguous. Key names can be typed in either case. The prefix character can be changed to any standard character, and typing it twice sends the literal prefix character to OLS.
sections.plainLanguage: Type regular keys normally, but special keys need a prefix character, the key name, and a space, like a shortcut command.

sections.title: NETOLS Commands and Limitations
sections.content:
NETOLS interprets several special commands: HELP shows available keys and commands, PREFIX allows changing the prefix character, SHIFT and UNSHIFT control shift modes, FULLDUPLEX and HALFDUPLEX set the connection mode, STATE shows connection status, and LOGOUT closes the session.

Telnet users should understand the limitations: all curvilinear display and graphical output are suppressed, special user-created characters display is disabled, Greek characters display as lowercase a-z, and operations assuming a fixed-screen display (like editors) behave differently since Telnet is a continuous scrolling medium.
sections.plainLanguage: Some special commands control the connection, but graphics and fancy screen tricks do not work over Telnet.
